target.title: Decoding spectrotemporal features of overt and covert speech from the human cortex

read.pdf: Table 1 and Figs. 1–13 captions/descriptions in text.txt; separate PDF not inspected

entries.text: The cohort comprised seven epilepsy-surgery patients with implanted subdural ECoG arrays.
entries.condition: Clinical ECoG cohort; recordings during overt reading, covert reading, and resting control; n=7.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Subjects and Data Acquisition

entries.text: All subjects were described as cognitively normal and functionally independent; Table 1 reports individual clinical profiles.
entries.condition: Seven patients undergoing clinical monitoring for epilepsy; individual age, sex, intelligence scores, language lateralization, seizure focus, and grid/strip sites are tabulated.

entries.text: Subdural platinum-iridium electrodes were 4 mm in diameter, had 2.3 mm exposed, and were spaced 0.6–1 cm apart.
entries.unit: mm diameter; mm exposed; cm inter-electrode distance
entries.condition: Ad-Tech/PMT subdural grids; clinical grid placement and monitoring duration were determined by clinical requirements.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Subjects and Data Acquisition

entries.text: ECoG was acquired at 9600 Hz, downsampled to 1000 Hz, band-pass filtered at 0.5–200 Hz, notch-filtered at 60/120/180 Hz, rereferenced to common average, and converted to 70–150 Hz high-gamma envelopes with a Hilbert transform.
entries.condition: Seven 16-channel g.USBamp devices; visual rejection of ictal intervals and noisy channels; common-average rereferencing; high-gamma extraction after filtering.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Subjects and Data Acquisition

entries.text: The microphone was placed within 10 cm of the face and rated for 80–12000 Hz voice recordings; an eye tracker checked covert-task compliance.
entries.unit: cm; Hz microphone bandwidth; mV/Pa sensitivity
entries.condition: Dynamic Samson R21s microphone recorded the participant's own voice synchronously with ECoG; Tobii T60 eye tracker used for compliance monitoring.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Subjects and Data Acquisition

entries.text: Subjects read the same scrolling texts aloud and silently, plus a resting-state control; scrolling was 42–76 words/min and runs lasted 6–8 min, repeated 2–3 times.
entries.condition: Text excerpts were historical political speeches or a children's story; scroll rate was adjusted before recording to attention, cognitive/verbal ability, and comfort. Rest was recorded in a separate session for baseline control.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Experimental Paradigms

entries.text: The model predicted two acoustic target representations: a 32-bin spectrogram and 60 modulation features (5 scales × 12 rates).
entries.unit: features; frequency bins; Hz acoustic center frequencies; cycles/octave; Hz modulation rates
entries.condition: Spectrogram: 128-channel auditory filterbank downsampled to 32 log-spaced bins, 180–7000 Hz. Modulation: 2-D wavelet features over 0.5–8 cycles/octave and 1–32 Hz, averaged over frequency to 5 scales × 12 rates.
entries.quote:
In summary, the neural decoding model predicted 32 spectral frequency features and 60
rate and scale features in the spectrogram-based and modulation-
based speech representation, respectively.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Auditory Speech Representations

entries.text: A linear decoder mapped high-gamma activity from each electrode and time lag to speech features, using lags from −500 to +500 ms.
entries.condition: The model sums activity across electrodes and temporal lags for each output speech feature; overt speech model is used for reconstruction.
entries.quote: The decoding model was a linear mapping between neural activity and the speech representation (Figure 2A).
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: Parameters were fit by gradient-descent iterative linear regression with early stopping; 4–7 jackknife models' parameter estimates were averaged.
entries.condition: Models were fit separately by jackknife resampling; averaged estimates formed the final decoder. The STRFLab MATLAB toolbox was used.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: Early stopping monitored out-of-sample prediction accuracy on 10% of the training data and stopped after 30 iterations without improvement.
entries.unit: % of training data; consecutive iterations without improvement
entries.condition: The monitored data determined the early-stopping criterion; an independent 10% testing set was evaluated after fitting.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: Neural and speech data were synchronized, downsampled to 100 Hz, and standardized to zero mean and unit standard deviation before fitting.
entries.unit: Hz; standardized mean; standardized standard deviation
entries.condition: The paper does not say whether standardization parameters were estimated on training data only or on a broader dataset; see t52.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: Training targets were auditory features of each subject's own overt, self-generated speech paired with overt-condition high-gamma activity.
entries.condition: The trained overt-speech model was later applied to covert and resting-state neural data; no covert acoustic target was used for model fitting.
entries.quote: we used a similar neural decoding model trained on sounds from self-generated overt speech.

entries.text: The authors applied the same overt-trained model to covert-speech and resting-state activity without describing covert retraining or recalibration.
entries.condition: Within-subject decoding; overt-trained weights applied to the corresponding subject's covert and baseline-control activity.
entries.quote: the same model (Equation 1) was applied to data from the covert condition to predict speech features imagined by the subject
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Covert Speech Decoding

entries.text: Because covert speech has no synchronized acoustic output, the authors assumed it should match the spectrotemporal content of the same text spoken overtly and used that overt recording as ground truth.
entries.condition: Same story/text segments were read in both conditions; overt audio served as the covert reconstruction reference after time alignment.
entries.quote: we made the assumption that the covert speech representation should match the spectrotemporal content of overt speech.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Covert Speech Decoding

entries.text: Covert and baseline reconstructions were aligned to the overt reference with Euclidean-distance DTW, Rabiner-Juan type-3 steps, a 2-s Sakoe-Chiba window, and separate 30-s segments.
entries.unit: s maximum temporal offset/window; s segment duration
entries.condition: Allowed transitions were (1,2), (2,1), and (1,1); overt reconstructions did not use DTW unless otherwise stated.
entries.quote: the entire time series was broken into 30 s segments, and warping was applied on each individual pair of segments
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Dynamic Time Warping

entries.text: Reconstruction accuracy was Pearson correlation between original and reconstructed features, averaged across speech features and resamples; overt accuracy used the independent test set.
entries.unit: feature correlations per resample for spectrogram; feature correlations per resample for modulation
entries.condition: Overt evaluation used the independent test set. Covert evaluation first DTW-aligned predicted features to the corresponding original overt audio; baseline received matching DTW processing.

entries.text: Segment identification used 5-s speech segments and percentile rank among 24–140 candidate utterance segments; the worked examples used 123 segments.
entries.unit: s segment duration; candidate segments; segments in illustrated examples
entries.condition: Each reconstructed target was compared with original overt spectrogram references; pairwise DTW alignment and mean correlation generated similarity scores, which were ranked.

entries.text: Individual identification significance used a randomization null generated by shuffling candidate-set segment labels 10,000 times.
entries.condition: Identification ranks for overt, covert, and baseline conditions; segment duration was 5 s, chosen to exceed the representation's autocorrelation length.

entries.text: The paper does not specify an independent held-out covert block set; it says the overt-trained decoder was applied to covert-condition data and evaluates those reconstructions against overt references.
entries.condition: The 90/10 random block split is described for fitting and testing the overt decoder; no corresponding covert-condition partition is specified.
entries.quote: the same model (Equation 1) was applied to data from the covert condition to predict speech features imagined by the subject
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Covert Speech Decoding; Sec. Evaluation

entries.text: Overt spectrogram and modulation reconstruction each exceeded baseline in every individual subject at p<10^-5.
entries.condition: Subject-level overt reconstruction versus baseline; spectrogram Hotelling t-test and modulation Hotelling t-test, n=7 subjects.
entries.loc: Figs. 5, 7 captions; Sec. Results, Overt Speech

entries.text: The authors define chance percentile rank as 0.5 and perfect identification as 1.0.
entries.condition: Segment-identification metric; expected rank for chance and ideal rank for a correct match, respectively.

entries.text: Group mean overt spectrogram reconstruction accuracy was r=0.41, significantly above resting baseline.
entries.condition: Spectrogram model; overt speech; group mean across 7 subjects; compared with resting-state control; Fisher Z followed by paired two-sample t-test, p<10^-5.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.text: Group resting-control spectrogram reconstruction accuracy was r=0.00 and not significantly different from zero.
entries.condition: Spectrogram representation; resting-state baseline in the group comparison; one-sample t-test, p>0.1.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.text: Group-averaged overt spectrogram correlations across individual acoustic frequencies ranged approximately from 0.25 to 0.5.
entries.condition: Overt speech; group-averaged individual frequency bins; spectrogram model across the 7-subject cohort.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.text: For the illustrated subject, overt spectrogram identification had median rank 0.87 over 123 five-second segments, above chance.
entries.condition: One subject with left-hemisphere coverage; overt spectrogram reconstruction; randomization test p<10^-5; chance rank 0.5.
entries.loc: Fig. 6 caption; Sec. Results, Overt Speech

entries.condition: Across subjects; overt speech reconstruction; one-sided one-sample t-test, p<10^-6; chance=0.5.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.text: Group baseline segment-identification rank was 0.48 and was not significantly above chance.
entries.condition: Resting-state baseline; one-sided one-sample t-test, p>0.5; chance=0.5.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.text: Group mean overt modulation-feature reconstruction accuracy was r=0.55, significantly above resting baseline.
entries.condition: Modulation representation; overt speech; group mean across 7 subjects; compared with resting baseline; Fisher Z followed by paired two-sample t-test, p<10^-5.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Modulation-based Reconstruction

entries.text: Group modulation-feature resting-control reconstruction accuracy was r=0.02 and not significantly different from zero.
entries.condition: Modulation representation; resting-state baseline; group mean across 7 subjects; one-sample t-test, p>0.1.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Modulation-based Reconstruction

entries.text: For overt speech, group-averaged modulation reconstruction accuracy was highest for temporal modulation rates above 2 Hz.
entries.condition: Overt speech; modulation-based representation averaged across the 7 subjects; descriptive location of highest accuracy.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Modulation-based Reconstruction

entries.text: The authors report that the most informative sites for overt and covert feature decoding were in STG and pre-/post-central gyri.
entries.condition: Electrode-specific reconstruction accuracy compared with baseline; informative maps used p<0.05 with Bonferroni correction.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Informative Areas

entries.text: Covert spectrogram accuracy exceeded resting control in 5 of 7 individuals, with subject-level Hotelling tests at p<0.05.
entries.condition: Covert spectrogram reconstruction after DTW; comparison with equivalently DTW-aligned resting control; Hotelling t-test; remaining subjects p>0.05.
entries.quote:
The overall reconstruction accuracy for covert speech was signiﬁcantly higher than the control condition in
5 out of 7 individual subjects

entries.condition: Group-level spectrogram reconstruction; overt, covert, and DTW-aligned resting baseline; Fisher Z followed by one-way ANOVA.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Covert Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.condition: Group-level spectrogram feature correlations after DTW in all three conditions; covert<overt p<10^-5 and covert>baseline p<0.005; paired two-sample t-tests after Fisher Z.

rcovert = 0.34 < rovert =

entries.condition: One subject; covert reconstruction compared to overt references; randomization test p<0.005; chance rank 0.5.
entries.loc: Fig. 10 caption; Sec. Results, Covert Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.text: The illustrated subject's covert baseline identification rank was 0.47 and was not significant.
entries.condition: Resting-state baseline in the same 123-segment illustrated example; randomization test p>0.5; chance rank 0.5.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Covert Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.text: Group covert spectrogram identification rank was 0.55 versus chance 0.5, p<0.05; baseline rank was 0.48, p>0.5.

entries.condition: Modulation-based covert reconstruction; subject-level Hotelling t-test against baseline after DTW alignment.
entries.quote:
Reconstruction accuracy for the modulation-based covert speech
condition was signiﬁcant in 4 out of 7 individuals (p <

Figure 9B).
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Covert Speech, Modulation-based Reconstruction

entries.condition: Group-level modulation reconstruction; overt, covert, and DTW-aligned resting baseline; one-way ANOVA.

entries.condition: Group-level modulation feature correlations after DTW in all three conditions; covert<overt p<10^-5 and covert>baseline p<0.005; paired two-sample t-tests after Fisher Z.

entries.text: At the electrode level, overt-versus-covert condition effects were F(1,116)=19.6 for spectrogram and F(1,156)=16.9 for modulation.
entries.condition: Electrodes selected as significant in overt, covert, or both regions; p<0.05 Bonferroni threshold; condition effect p<10^-6 spectrogram and p<10^-4 modulation.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Covert Speech, Informative Areas

entries.text: At single electrodes, overt-minus-baseline mean differences were 0.06 spectrogram and 0.10 modulation; covert-minus-baseline differences were 0.006 and 0.01.
entries.unit: mean Pearson-r difference: overt spectrogram; overt modulation; covert spectrogram; covert modulation
entries.condition: Single-electrode analysis of informative areas; overt and covert feature reconstruction compared with baseline; described with the experimental-condition effects.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Covert Speech, Informative Areas

entries.text: Anatomical-region main effects were F(2,116)=3.22 for spectrogram and F(2,156)=3.4 for modulation, but post-hoc Bonferroni tests found no pairwise regional difference at p=0.05.
entries.unit: F(2,116) spectrogram; F(2,156) modulation; post-hoc p threshold; mean r difference: STG spectrogram/modulation; precentral spectrogram/modulation; postcentral spectrogram/modulation
entries.condition: Single-electrode informative sites; regions were STG, pre-central gyrus, and post-central gyrus; two-way ANOVA and Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc t-tests. The listed regional differences were not significant at p=0.05.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Covert Speech, Informative Areas

entries.text: The condition-by-region interaction was F(2,156)=3.6, p<0.05 for modulation and F(2,116)=2.92, p=0.058 for spectrogram; modulation STG overt-minus-covert difference was 0.12, p<10^-5.
entries.unit: F(2,156) modulation; F(2,116) spectrogram; p-value; mean Pearson-r differences for STG, precentral, postcentral; p-value
entries.condition: Electrode-level two-way ANOVA by experimental condition and anatomical region; modulation differences at precentral (0.06) and postcentral (0.02) were not significant (p>0.05).
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Covert Speech, Informative Areas

entries.text: The authors present transfer of an overt-trained decoder to covert speech as evidence that covert auditory features can be decoded from ECoG and that overt/covert speech have a partially shared neural substrate.
entries.condition: Evidence is based on within-subject reconstructions of spectrogram and modulation features; covert estimates are compared with overt reference audio after DTW.
entries.quote: These results provide evidence that auditory representations of covert speech can be reconstructed from models that are built from an overt speech data set, supporting a partially shared neural substrate.

entries.text: The authors claim covert feature reconstruction is above control, while consistently reporting lower predictive accuracy than overt speech.
entries.condition: Group and subject-level results; covert is evaluated against baseline after the same DTW processing; spectrogram and modulation correlations are reported separately in t31 and t37.

entries.text: The authors say group covert identification was only marginally significant and only one of seven subjects had individually significant covert identification.
entries.unit: subjects; group covert p-value; group overt p-value
entries.condition: Segment identification against chance; group-level test and individual-subject results; covert performance weaker than overt.

entries.text: They identify alignment of covert reconstructions to a reference as a major difficulty because speaking rate, pronunciation, and errors can produce suboptimal alignment.
entries.condition: Covert reconstruction compared with an overt reference; the paper suggests improved alignment or speech-recognition methods as future work.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that their simple model assumes covert auditory imagery is equivalent to overt auditory representation and may miss systematic differences.
entries.condition: Same overt-trained mapping is applied to covert activity; authors propose future model adjustment if covert-specific spectrotemporal differences are established.

entries.text: They state that weaker covert accuracy may reflect lower high-gamma signal-to-noise ratio, but the contributions of SNR and representational differences remain unresolved.
entries.condition: Overt/covert high-gamma activity and reconstruction-accuracy comparison; proposed explanation is tentative, not resolved by this study.
entries.quote:
Future work is needed to determine the rel-
ative contributions of SNR vs. differences in the underlying neural
representations to account for discrepancies between overt and
covert speech reconstruction accuracy.

entries.text: The authors caution that DTW can artificially increase correlation, including for noise, and therefore compare covert and baseline data with equivalent processing.
entries.condition: DTW applied to covert and baseline reconstructions; baseline correlation may exceed zero because of the algorithm's flexibility.

entries.text: The authors describe the results as a basis for developing brain-based communication for patients with disabling neurological conditions, not as a deployed communication system.
entries.condition: Discussion frames communication as future development; the evaluated system reconstructs auditory features from implanted ECoG in epilepsy patients.

entries.text: The data were divided into 7-s blocks; 90% were randomly assigned to training and 10% to an independent test set.
entries.condition: Random block-level partition was used to retain temporal correlations; validation comprised 10% of the training portion for early stopping.
entries.quote: From these blocks, 90% were randomly partitioned into a training set and 10% into a testing set.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: The random block split is described, but no random seed or number of repeated train/test partitions is reported; the 4–7 jackknife fits are not stated to be repeated random splits.
entries.condition: Random 90/10 partition of 7-s blocks; number of random split repetitions and seeds for partitioning, model fitting, and randomization are not specified.
entries.quote: From these blocks, 90% were randomly partitioned into a training set and 10% into a testing set.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: No held-out-speaker or cross-subject test is reported; the analysis evaluates subjects individually and reports group summaries, so generalization to unseen speakers is untested.
entries.condition: The paper describes subject-level results for seven participants but does not specify a speaker-disjoint split or an external participant test cohort.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Overt Speech, Spectrogram-based Reconstruction

entries.text: The paper states that data were standardized before fitting but does not say whether the mean and standard deviation were estimated from training data only or included test data.
entries.condition: Zero-mean, unit-standard-deviation standardization is reported; scope of fitting the normalization parameters is not stated.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: The paper identifies the early-stopping monitor as 10% of training data, but does not describe any additional validation or model-selection dataset or choices beyond early stopping.
entries.condition: The independent 10% test set is said to be used for final evaluation; the exact relationship of jackknife fits to the validation subset is not detailed.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: The paper does not report a held-out session, held-out story, or separate external test set; the stated test is a random partition of blocks from the recorded data.
entries.condition: The same stories were used in overt and covert conditions; exact story/session composition of training, validation, and test partitions is not specified.
entries.quote: subjects read the same stories both aloud (overt) and silently (covert).
entries.loc: Abstract; Sec. Materials and Methods, Decoding Model and Reconstruction Procedure

entries.text: Chance rank is specified for segment identification, but the paper does not give a standalone numeric chance threshold for DTW-aligned reconstruction correlations; it uses resting-state control as comparator.
entries.condition: DTW can raise baseline correlation above zero; covert significance is assessed against a baseline processed with the same alignment procedure.

entries.text: The described pipeline outputs continuous acoustic-feature reconstructions and segment-identification ranks; no language model or language-model-assisted decoding stage is described.
entries.condition: Spectrogram or modulation feature output; the paper discusses HMMs only as a possible future alignment/recognition aid, not as part of the evaluated pipeline.
entries.quote: the neural decoding model predicted 32 spectral frequency features and 60 rate and scale features
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and Methods, Auditory Speech Representations; Sec. Discussion

entries.text: No user confirmation or acceptance step is described or evaluated; output is assessed through feature correlation and segment identification.
entries.condition: Offline experimental reconstruction and statistical evaluation; no user-facing interaction protocol is reported.

entries.text: No online correction, user adaptation, or error-repair interaction is described or evaluated.
entries.condition: The decoder is evaluated offline on recorded ECoG; future improvement discussion concerns model/alignment changes rather than a participant correction interface.

entries.text: No real-time deployment, communication rate, prospective user trial, or evaluation in patients with disabling communication conditions is reported.
entries.condition: Recordings were made from seven epilepsy patients in clinical monitoring; communication use is proposed as future development.

entries.text: PCC=0.423 is the correlation between phoneme accuracy and W score for overt EEG when silence ('sil') is excluded; including silence gives 0.162.
entries.condition: Fig. 7 representative subject; overt EEG; W score excluding 'sil'; 30 unseen test sentences per participant in the study; 15 healthy participants overall; decoding/LM and seeds not specified for this correlation.

entries.text: The primary dataset comprises 15 healthy participants and synchronized EEG, EMG, and audio for 474 English sentences (460 MOCHA-TIMIT plus 14 additional), across overt, whispered, and imagined modes; the EEG cap has 128 channels and EMG has 10 channels.
entries.condition: Per-subject personalized decoding; vocabulary is English; all 474 sentence items were performed in each speech mode; 15 healthy participants (8 Korean-native, 7 English-native); decoding used EEG alone or EEG+EMG; HiFi-GAN/DeepSpeech are used downstream; seeds not reported.
entries.quote: EEG, EMG, and audio signals of 474

entries.text: For each speech mode, the 474 trials were split into 444 training and 30 test trials; test sentences were unseen and there was no overlap or repetition between splits.
entries.condition: Split is sentence-level and evaluated per participant (15 healthy participants; 30 test sentences each); English vocabulary; not a subject-held-out split; decoding model is subject-specific; seeds not reported.
entries.quote: with no overlap or repetition between the datasets.

entries.text: Yes: whispered and imagined inputs use the overt recording of the same sentence as target/reference audio, so each covert test sentence has a sentence-matched overt reference.
entries.condition: Covert modes are whispered and imagined; 30 unseen English test sentences per participant; the three modes were recorded for each sentence; personalized decoding; seeds not reported.
entries.quote: sentences were employed as target audio

entries.text: The matched overt audio is a reference for the covert-mode target/evaluation, but the recorded audio and target sentence are withheld from the model during inference.
entries.condition: Applies to inference for all modes; evaluation is on 30 unseen sentences per participant; HiFi-GAN synthesizes predicted MFCC and DeepSpeech performs ASR; no external language model or random seeds are reported.

entries.text: Real-time 125,000-word inner-speech decoding on T15 and T16 yielded aggregate WERs of 26%–54% (95% CIs 15.5%–32.3% and 42.5%–65.3%).
entries.condition: Self-paced cued inner speech; Switchboard sentences; 125,000-word CMU dictionary vocabulary; RNN with CTC and n-gram LM. The prose does not map each WER endpoint to a participant.

entries.text: The three 125k closed-loop sessions evaluated 69 sentences total; T15's decoder retrained throughout evaluation and T16's retrained after decoding each cued sentence, so these are adaptive-model results, not a frozen-decoder test.
entries.condition: T15 sessions: 15 and 25 sentences; T16: 29; Switchboard test sentences did not overlap training. Kaldi n-gram LM with CMU dictionary; T15 additionally used OPT transformer rescoring. Seed count for these real-time 125k results is not stated.

entries.text: This clinical result used intracortical microelectrode arrays in motor cortex, not ECoG; the 125k evaluations were in T15 and T16, each with four 64-channel arrays in precentral regions.
entries.value: 4 participants; T15 and T16 in the 125k test
entries.condition: BrainGate2 cohort T12, T15, T16, T17; T15/T16 had four 64-channel intracortical arrays each; large-vocabulary tests used T15/T16.

entries.text: The paper describes real-time, self-paced decoding but reports no numerical neural-to-output or end-to-end latency; WER is an error metric, not a communication-rate measurement.
entries.condition: 125,000-word real-time inner-speech evaluation; no latency in milliseconds or words-per-minute result stated.

entries.text: Inner speech was preferred for lower effort and comfort and may bypass breathing-control limits; speed comparable to normal speech is a proposed benefit, not a demonstrated rate result.
entries.condition: Comparison with attempted speech in participants with severe dysarthria; no measured communication speed reported.

entries.text: Free-form thought yielded some decodable words, but complete intelligible sentences were not accurately decoded; the four-person findings may not generalize across users.
entries.condition: Free-form prompted thinking versus instructed inner speech; clinical cohort of four participants.

entries.text: A keyword unlock was tested online with T12 at 98.75% success; imagery-silenced training is a separate safeguard that remained unverified in online real-time decoding.
entries.condition: T12; real-time keyword-gated inner-speech BCI; 80 trials. Imagery-silenced decoder was evaluated offline only.

entries.text: Neural input consisted of spike-derived normalized firing rates recorded from a Neurotrophic Electrode in speech-related motor cortex during attempted speech.
